[2019 fall ms applied — problem 5]

July temperatures (°F) in New Brunswick and Piscataway on the same randomly chosen date in each of 7 years; measures in different years independent, but the two cities on the same day are not. (A) Give point estimates of each city's mean July temperature and the standard errors. (B) Give a 95% prediction interval for next year's New Brunswick temperature. (C) Test whether the two cities' mean July temperatures are equal at level 0.05.

response.text:
The numerical data values are not included in the prompt, so numerical estimates cannot be computed. But the correct statistical procedures are as follows.

Let

\[
X_i=\text{New Brunswick July temperature in year }i,
\qquad 
Y_i=\text{Piscataway July temperature in year }i,
\]

for \(i=1,\dots,7\). The pairs \((X_i,Y_i)\) are independent across years, but \(X_i\) and \(Y_i\) within the same year may be dependent.

Let

\[
\bar X=\frac1{7}\sum_{i=1}^7 X_i,\qquad 
\bar Y=\frac1{7}\sum_{i=1}^7 Y_i,
\]

and

\[
s_X^2=\frac1{6}\sum_{i=1}^7 (X_i-\bar X)^2,\qquad
s_Y^2=\frac1{6}\sum_{i=1}^7 (Y_i-\bar Y)^2.
\]

---

## (A) Point estimates and standard errors

The point estimate of the mean July temperature in New Brunswick is

\[
\widehat{\mu}_X=\bar X.
\]

Its standard error is

\[
\operatorname{SE}(\bar X)=\frac{s_X}{\sqrt{7}}.
\]

Similarly, the point estimate of the mean July temperature in Piscataway is

\[
\widehat{\mu}_Y=\bar Y,
\]

with standard error

\[
\operatorname{SE}(\bar Y)=\frac{s_Y}{\sqrt{7}}.
\]

The dependence between the two cities on the same date does not affect the standard error of either individual sample mean. It does matter when comparing the two means.

---

## (B) 95% prediction interval for next year’s New Brunswick temperature

Assume the New Brunswick temperatures are approximately normally distributed. For a future observation \(X_{\text{new}}\), the prediction interval is

\[
\bar X \pm t_{0.975,6} \, s_X \sqrt{1+\frac{1}{7}}.
\]

Since

\[
t_{0.975,6}\approx 2.447,
\]

the 95% prediction interval is

\[
\boxed{
\bar X \pm 2.447\, s_X\sqrt{\frac{8}{7}}
}.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
\left(
\bar X-2.447\,s_X\sqrt{\frac{8}{7}},
\,
\bar X+2.447\,s_X\sqrt{\frac{8}{7}}
\right).
}
\]

---

## (C) Test whether the two cities have equal mean July temperatures

Because the temperatures are observed in pairs on the same randomly chosen date each year, this is a paired two-sample test.

Define the paired differences

\[
D_i=X_i-Y_i,\qquad i=1,\dots,7.
\]

We test

\[
H_0:\mu_D=0
\]

against

\[
H_a:\mu_D\neq 0,
\]

where

\[
\mu_D=\mu_X-\mu_Y.
\]

Compute

\[
\bar D=\frac1{7}\sum_{i=1}^7 D_i
\]

and

\[
s_D^2=\frac1{6}\sum_{i=1}^7 (D_i-\bar D)^2.
\]

The test statistic is

\[
T=\frac{\bar D}{s_D/\sqrt{7}}.
\]

Under \(H_0\), assuming the paired differences are approximately normally distributed,

\[
T\sim t_6.
\]

At significance level \(0.05\), the two-sided rejection rule is

\[
|T|>t_{0.975,6}.
\]

Since

\[
t_{0.975,6}\approx 2.447,
\]

we reject \(H_0\) if

\[
\boxed{
\left|\frac{\bar D}{s_D/\sqrt{7}}\right|>2.447.
}
\]

Equivalently, the \(p\)-value is

\[
p=2P\left(t_6\ge |T|\right).
\]

Reject \(H_0\) if \(p<0.05\); otherwise, fail to reject \(H_0\).

The important point is that this must be a paired \(t\)-test, not an independent two-sample \(t\)-test, because New Brunswick and Piscataway temperatures measured on the same date are dependent.
